title: Carbonara with Guanciale and Mushrooms
subtitle: Roman classic · ready in 25 minutes
description: A traditional Roman carbonara built on rendered guanciale, egg yolks, and Pecorino, with earthy mushrooms folded in. No cream, no garlic.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to a boil and add the {{salt}}. Keep it at a rolling boil — you'll need the starchy water later.
Whisk the {{yolks}} and {{egg}} with about three-quarters of the {{pecorino}} and most of the {{pepper}} into a thick, pale paste. Set aside.

Add the {{guanciale}} to a cold, large skillet and set over medium heat. Render slowly until the fat is liquid and the pieces are golden and crisp. Remove with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat behind.

Raise the heat to medium-high and add the {{mushrooms}} to the rendered fat. Cook undisturbed for a minute, then stir occasionally until deeply browned and any liquid has evaporated. Turn off the heat and return the {{guanciale}} to the pan.
Cook the {{spaghetti}} until just shy of al dente. Reserve at least 250ml of pasta water before draining.
Add the drained pasta to the off-heat skillet and toss to coat. Whisk 2–3 tablespoons of hot pasta water into the egg mixture to temper it, then pour it over the pasta.

Toss vigorously off the heat, adding splashes of reserved pasta water until the sauce turns glossy and clings. The residual warmth cooks the eggs into a creamy sauce — never return it to direct heat or it will scramble.
Plate immediately and top with the remaining {{pecorino}} and {{pepper}}. Serve at once.

notes: All the egg work happens off the heat. If the pan is too hot when the eggs go in, they'll scramble.
Trim the tough rind off the guanciale before cutting, but drop it into the pan while rendering for extra flavour, then discard it before the mushrooms go in.
No garlic and no cream — the guanciale fat and sharp Pecorino carry all the flavour.
Pecorino Romano is traditional and sharper than Parmesan. If it's too salty for you, do half Pecorino, half Parmigiano-Reggiano.
Don't add salt to the sauce — the guanciale and cheese are already salty.
